# mergeset

Which of these branches can be merged together?

Given a base commit and *n* candidate changes — branches, pull requests, commits — `mergeset` finds the **maximal sets** that merge cleanly and still pass validation, and the minimal **conflicts** that stop the rest.

```bash
pip install mergeset
python -m mergeset branches feat-a feat-b feat-c --base main
```

**Driving it from an agent?** `mergeset` ships the skill an agent needs to drive it well — ask the free oracles before spending a test run, what a green report does *not* mean, and why a run’s output never goes into a repository.

```bash
gh skill install i2mint/mergeset mergeset --agent claude-code   # or copilot, cursor, codex, gemini
```

The same skill is inside the wheel, so `pip install mergeset` already has it — `mergeset install-skills` links it into an agent’s directory, offline.

```python
from mergeset import analyze, branch_changes, markdown_report

changes = list(branch_changes(".", ["feat-a", "feat-b", "feat-c"], base="main"))
print(markdown_report(analyze(".", changes)))
```

You get a merge plan: merge these, in this order, and here is what you lose — plus, for everything dropped, whether it was a textual conflict (and in which files) or a test failure (and which tests).

## Why it is not just “try every subset”

Evaluating a subset means merging it and running a test suite. That is minutes, and there are `2**n` subsets. So `mergeset` spends its evaluations the way a person would if each one cost real money.

**Ask the cheap oracles first.** Nothing expensive runs until everything free has had its say: a change whose own CI is red is a conflict of size one; `git merge-tree --write-tree` finds textual conflicts in milliseconds without ever creating a working tree; and changes touching disjoint files form independent subproblems that are solved separately and combined.

**Never evaluate the same set twice.** Every evaluation is appended to `~/.local/share/mergeset/evaluations/<repo>.jsonl`, which is the single source of truth. Each row records the base and head shas it was merged at, and only rows about the current commits are reused, so rewriting a branch never answers from its old tree. Re-running is nearly free, a crashed run resumes, and reports regenerate without re-running anything. The log also propagates monotonicity: a passing set marks all its subsets good, a failing set marks all its supersets bad.

**Search like a SAT solver, not like a loop.** A failure is shrunk to a minimal conflict by QuickXplain (`O(k log n)` evaluations instead of `O(n)`), and the next candidate to try is the complement of the cheapest minimal hitting set of all conflicts found so far — Reiter’s hitting-set duality, which says exactly that complements of maximal good sets *are* the minimal hitting sets of the conflicts.

**Weights mean “cost of dropping this”.** When something has to go, the tool drops the cheapest work, not the first thing it thought of.

## Where the output goes

Reports, evaluation logs, raw validation output and captured fixtures all land in an **artifact store**, never in a repository:

```default
~/.local/share/mergeset/            # $MERGESET_DATA_DIR overrides the root
    reports/<repo>/<timestamp>/     # REPORT.md, report.html — one key per run
    evaluations/<repo>.jsonl        # the append-only log — the source of truth
    logs/                           # raw build/test/lint output
    fixtures/                       # captured failures kept as regression tests
```

This is not tidiness. Everything `mergeset` produces is **captured from the repository it analysed** — source paths, symbol names, stack traces with verbatim code, branch names, PR metadata. Written into that repository (or into `mergeset`’s own), one `git add .` publishes it. This project has already published a private repository’s internals to a public one exactly that way, so the default is now a location no `git add` can reach.

Each kind is a plain `MutableMapping[str, str]`, so the backend is one keyword argument:

```python
from mergeset import analyze, artifact_mall

# Local files, the default:
analyze(repo, changes)

# The same run, with every artifact in S3 — one keyword argument, no other change:
s3 = artifact_mall(store_factory=lambda kind, root: S3Store(bucket, prefix=kind))
analyze(repo, changes, artifacts=s3)
```

A factory is handed the **kind and the root separately**, never a joined filesystem path: a backend with no filesystem should not have to parse one out.

`--report-dir` still writes wherever you point it — an explicit choice, not a default. Without it, each run gets its own key, so re-analysing a repository never overwrites the answer you are comparing against.

Reports render as Markdown and HTML by default, and PDF on request:

```bash
python -m mergeset prs OWNER/REPO --report-format markdown html pdf   # needs mergeset[pdf]
```

The PDF is rendered from the Markdown, not the HTML — the HTML report draws itself from an embedded JSON blob at load time, so a print pipeline that does not run JavaScript would give you a blank page that looks fine until someone opens it.

## Progressive disclosure

The call above takes no configuration and works. Every piece of it is one keyword argument away from being replaced.

| you want to change           | keyword                                                                                                                                                                      |
|------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| where changes come from      | `mergeset.sources` — `branch_changes`, `pr_changes`, `commit_changes`, or any iterable of `Change`                                                                           |
| where artifacts are kept     | `mergeset.storage` — `artifact_store(kind, store_factory=...)`; local files by default, S3 by passing a different factory                                                    |
| what counts as “works”       | `validate=` — `pytest_validation()`, `command_validation('make test')`, `js_validation(...)`, `staged_validation([...])`, `act_validation()`, `callable_validation(my_func)` |
| how much it may spend        | `max_evaluations=`, `max_seconds=`, `max_sets=` — partial results are always returned and labelled partial                                                                   |
| what dropping a change costs | `weight=` — any `Change -> float`                                                                                                                                            |
| where the log lives          | `log=` / `log_path=` — anything with `append` and `__iter__`                                                                                                                 |
| conflict resolution          | `resolver=claude_code_resolver()` — flagged, never silent                                                                                                                    |

## Real repositories are messier than the theory

Three things break the clean picture, and `mergeset` handles each explicitly rather than pretending.

**Stacked PRs.** A PR opened against another PR’s branch already contains it, so subsets are not free: a valid set must be *downward-closed* under the parent relation — and stacks branch, so this is a forest, not a chain. `mergeset` closes sets before evaluating them, merges only the *tips* (merging a tip brings its ancestors), and charges the cost of a change’s whole descendant cone when deciding what to drop. On a 15-PR forest this also cuts the search space from 32768 subsets to 576.

**A green PR that will not land.** GitHub’s `mergeable` and CI status are computed against the PR’s *own* base branch. If that branch has moved on, a PR can be green and “CLEAN” on GitHub and still refuse to merge onto `main`. `mergeset` ignores the forge’s verdict whenever the bases disagree, and checks by actually merging.

**Monotonicity is a prior, not a law.** A change can contain the fix that makes another one work, and flaky tests break closure outright. Violations are detected and reported loudly rather than silently trusted; `flake_tolerant(validate, retries=1)` is the cheap mitigation.

## Validation is a sequence, not a command

Real projects do not have “the test command”. They have an install step (slow, and only needed when the lockfile moved), a build step that is a *prerequisite* of testing rather than part of it, then tests, then lint. A single pass/fail bit throws away the distinction you most need — “failed to build” is not “tests failed”.

From the CLI, the same thing, repeatable and ordered:

```bash
python -m mergeset prs OWNER/REPO --repo . \
    --validate-stage 'setup:pnpm install --frozen-lockfile' \
                     'build:pnpm run build' \
                     'test:pnpm run test' \
                     'lint:pnpm run lint' \
    --validate-fingerprint 'setup:pnpm-lock.yaml' \
    --validate-optional lint \
    --reuse-worktree /tmp/mergeset-wt
```

An optional stage’s failure is recorded but does not veto the set — for a lint the project runs as a separate job rather than a gate.

The evaluation log reuses a verdict only when the commits and the validator are the same, and “the validator” means its command text. When the command runs a script that lives outside the repository (`--validate-command 'python ~/checks/smoke.py'`), add `--validate-input ~/checks/smoke.py` (repeatable; a directory works too): the script’s contents then join the validator’s fingerprint, and editing it re-runs the sets instead of reusing the old script’s verdicts. In the library, `command_validation`, `pytest_validation`, `act_validation`, `staged_validation` and `js_validation` take `inputs=[...]`. The contents are read when the validator is made and checked again around every run: an input edited mid-run stops the run instead of recording a verdict under the old fingerprint.

From the library:

```python
from mergeset import ValidationStage, staged_validation, file_fingerprint

validate = staged_validation(
    [
        ValidationStage(
            "setup",
            "pnpm install --frozen-lockfile",
            fingerprint=file_fingerprint("pnpm-lock.yaml"),
        ),
        ValidationStage("build", "pnpm run build"),
        ValidationStage("test", "pnpm run test"),
        ValidationStage("lint", "pnpm run lint", required=False),
    ]
)
analyze(repo, changes, validate=validate, reuse_worktree="/tmp/scratch-wt")
```

The fingerprinted stage runs only when its inputs actually change, and `reuse_worktree` keeps one tree across the whole run — so an expensive install is paid once, not once per evaluation.

## Tiered validation: screen cheaply, confirm expensively

When the real check is too slow to run on every candidate set (a browser suite, a container build), give `mergeset` a ladder of validators, cheapest first. The first tier screens every set the search touches; each later tier only confirms the sets its predecessor left standing, so the expensive suite runs on a handful of sets instead of dozens. Each tier keeps its own evaluation log, because a cheap PASS is not evidence about an expensive tier.

```bash
python -m mergeset prs OWNER/REPO --repo . \
    --validate-stage 'setup:pnpm install --frozen-lockfile' 'test:pnpm run test' \
    --validate-fingerprint 'setup:pnpm-lock.yaml' \
    --tier unit 'e2e:pnpm run e2e' \
    --tier-cost 'e2e:300' \
    --confirm-budget-seconds 1800 \
    --must-include pr42
```

`--tier 'name:command'` is a tier that runs one command. A bare name (`unit` above) is the tier the `--validate-*` flags describe: stages compose *inside* a validator, tiers compose *across* validators. `--tier-cost` declares what an untimed tier costs per run, so it is not scheduled as if it were cheap; `--confirm-budget-seconds` and `--confirm-max-runs` bound what the deeper tiers may spend, admitting runs on the pessimistic estimate. `--must-include` also reports the best plan that keeps a given change, which is a different question from the maximal sets and is answered alongside them. The report says how deep validation got, what each tier spent, and whether each price was measured or declared. The library entry point is `analyze_tiered`.

## Output

- **Markdown report** — the merge plans first, then what stops the rest, then the evidence.
- **Self-contained HTML** — one file, no build step, no network: the conflict graph (textual vs validation conflicts distinguished), the plans, and the evaluation log.
- **Exit status** — `0` when the run finished or stopped on its budget; `3` when a search aborted (the report says `ABORTED` and why, and is still printed in full: it is what was established, not an answer). Refusals before a run starts keep `0`.
- **Integration branches** — `--integration-branches` creates a local `integration/<date>-<k>` per maximal set so you can test one by hand. It only ever creates *new local* branches; it never touches an existing branch and never pushes.

## Requirements

- Python ≥ 3.10, git ≥ 2.38 (for `git merge-tree --write-tree`; checked at startup with a message telling you how to fix it).
- `gh`, authenticated, only if you use the pull-request source.
- Whatever your validation command needs. Capabilities are checked up front rather than failing halfway through a long run.

## Reading further

[`docs/adr/`]() records every non-obvious design choice and why — one numbered ADR per decision, with an index. [`docs/RESEARCH.md`]() covers the MUS/MSS literature this is built on, the merge-queue prior art, and what was deliberately not depended on.

# _autosummary/mergeset.analysis.html.md

# mergeset.analysis

The facade: one call that goes from a repository to a merge plan.

`analyze` is the “simple thing made simple” entry point. It wires together the
pieces — sources, cheap pre-oracles, file-overlap decomposition, the expensive
oracle, the log, the search — with defaults that work out of the box, and every
piece stays replaceable by one keyword argument.

The order of operations is the whole point, because it is the order of *cost*:

1. free: per-change CI status (a red singleton is a conflict of size one);
2. milliseconds: pairwise `git merge-tree` textual conflicts;
3. milliseconds: file-overlap components — independent subproblems;
4. minutes each: the real merge-and-test oracle, only on what is left.

### Functions

| [`analyze`](_autosummary/mergeset.analysis.html.md#mergeset.analysis.analyze)(repo, changes, \*[, base, validate, ...])   | Find the maximal sets of `changes` that merge and validate on `base`.   |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`unmatched_log_notes`](_autosummary/mergeset.analysis.html.md#mergeset.analysis.unmatched_log_notes)(log, \*[, label])               | Say how many rows a pinned log is keeping but not using, and why.       |

### Classes

| [`Analysis`](_autosummary/mergeset.analysis.html.md#mergeset.analysis.Analysis)(repo, base, base_sha, changes[, ...])   | Everything a run learned.   |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------|

### *class* mergeset.analysis.Analysis(repo, base, base_sha, changes, head_shas=<factory>, maximal_sets=<factory>, conflicts=<factory>, textual_conflicts=<factory>, components=<factory>, files_by_change=<factory>, stacks=<factory>, merged_through=<factory>, weights=<factory>, own_weights=<factory>, singleton_conflicts=<factory>, components_combined=False, aborted_tier=None, unverified_sets=<factory>, log=None, tier_logs=<factory>, searches=<factory>, notes=<factory>)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Everything a run learned. Every field is derivable from `log` + git.

#### *property* aborted *: [str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str) | [None](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)*

Why a search stopped on an `ERROR`, or `None`.

An abort is not a budget stop (ADR 0017, 0036): the run could not do
what it was asked, and what it reports is only what it had established.

#### aborted_tier *: [str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str) | [None](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)* *= None*

The confirm tier whose search aborted, when one did after the screen
finished (`None`: the screen itself aborted, or nothing did).

#### *property* by_id *: [Dict](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Dict)[[str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str), [Change](_autosummary/mergeset.base.html.md#mergeset.base.Change)]*

Changes keyed by id.

#### components_combined *: [bool](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)* *= False*

Whether the per-component answers were trusted to combine, or whether a
global search had to verify them. See `analyze(component_local=...)`.

#### *property* evaluations *: [int](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)*

How many expensive evaluations this analysis rests on.

In a tiered run, those of the first tier (`log`); every tier’s count
is [`evaluations_by_tier`](_autosummary/mergeset.analysis.html.md#mergeset.analysis.Analysis.evaluations_by_tier), which is what the reports show.

Counted from the **log**, which is the source of truth, not from the
search state, which only knows what *this process* ran. Regenerating a
report from a complete log spends nothing, and the search-state number
then reads 0 — so the better the cache worked, the more the archived
report understated the work. A real 18-candidate run that cost 9
evaluations and 344 s reported “0 expensive evaluations spent”.

Rows are counted when they decided something about this candidate set:
a recorded PASS or FAIL (an ERROR established nothing) over a subset of
the changes in play (so an older run’s rows for a different candidate
set in the same log are not claimed as this analysis’s work). The base
check counts — it is an evaluation, and on a real project it is one of
the slowest.

#### *property* evaluations_by_tier *: [Dict](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Dict)[[str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str), [int](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)]*

[`evaluations`](_autosummary/mergeset.analysis.html.md#mergeset.analysis.Analysis.evaluations), per tier, cheapest first; empty when untiered.

#### *property* evaluations_this_run *: [int](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)*

How many expensive evaluations *this process* spent.

The number a progress display wants — 0 on a re-run is correct here and
misleading in a report. See [`evaluations`](_autosummary/mergeset.analysis.html.md#mergeset.analysis.Analysis.evaluations).

#### *property* exhausted *: [bool](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)*

True iff every component’s search finished rather than hit a budget.

#### head_shas *: [Dict](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Dict)[[str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str), [str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]*

Full head sha of each change, resolved once at the start. Everything that
merges uses these, never the refs, so what is recorded is what was merged.

#### merge_plan()

One entry per maximal set: what to merge, in what order, what it drops.

This is the deliverable — “merge these, in this order, and you lose these”.

* **Return type:**
  [`List`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.List)[[`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)]

#### merged_through *: [Dict](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Dict)[[str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str), [str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]*

The `stacks` edges whose child head really contains the parent’s head,
so merging the child brings the parent along. Only these let the oracle
merge a tip alone; any other parent is merged explicitly, or the row
would name a parent head that was never in the tree (#23).

#### own_weights *: [Dict](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Dict)[[str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str), [float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)]*

Cost of the change on its own, before the cone is accounted for.

#### *property* pinned_changes *: [List](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.List)[[Change](_autosummary/mergeset.base.html.md#mergeset.base.Change)]*

The changes with `head` replaced by the sha it resolved to.

A branch that moves mid-run must not have its new commits merged under
a row pinned to the old ones; merging the resolved shas rules that out.

#### singleton_conflicts *: [Dict](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Dict)[[str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str), [List](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.List)[[str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]]*

Changes that will not even merge onto base alone -> conflicting files.

#### tier_logs *: [Dict](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Dict)[[str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str), [EvaluationLog](_autosummary/mergeset.log.html.md#mergeset.log.EvaluationLog)]*

Each tier’s log, cheapest first, when validation was tiered
([`mergeset.analyze_tiered()`](_autosummary/mergeset.html.md#mergeset.analyze_tiered)); `log` is then the first of them.
Empty otherwise. What reports read to show every tier’s work, not only
the screen’s (i2mint/mergeset#29).

#### unverified_sets *: [List](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.List)[[frozenset](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#frozenset)]*

Sets reported without ever having been evaluated as a whole. Empty is the
normal case. See [`merge_plan()`](_autosummary/mergeset.analysis.html.md#mergeset.analysis.Analysis.merge_plan)’s `verified` and ADR 0025.

#### weights *: [Dict](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Dict)[[str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str), [float](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)]*

Cost of dropping each change *including its descendant cone*.

    to `<artifact root>/evaluations/<repo-slug>.jsonl` (see
    [`mergeset.storage`](_autosummary/mergeset.storage.html.md#module-mergeset.storage)), *outside* the analysed repository. Reusing
    an existing one makes a re-run nearly free. Only rows evaluated
    against the same base and heads, by the same validator, are reused
    (see ADR 0028 and [`mergeset.validation.fingerprint_of()`](_autosummary/mergeset.validation.html.md#mergeset.validation.fingerprint_of)).
  * **trust_unpinned** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`bool`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)]) – Reuse log rows written before rows recorded their

  * **decompose** ([`bool`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)) – Use file-overlap components to find conflicts cheaply. The
    components are always searched first, because a conflict found

    for any whole-repo test run\*\*, which can fail on generated
    artifacts, barrel exports, snapshots, type checks or project-wide
    lint that no changed-file overlap predicts. When false (the
    default), the combined result is verified by a global search seeded
    with every conflict the components found. `None` (the default)
    asks the validator: one may set `validate.component_local = True`
    to declare it, as [`merge_only_validation()`](_autosummary/mergeset.validation.html.md#mergeset.validation.merge_only_validation)
    does.
  * **check_base** ([`bool`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)) – Evaluate the base commit on its own before anything else, so
    a broken base or a misconfigured validator is a refusal rather than
    15 confident failures.
  * **use_ci_status** ([`bool`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)) – Treat a change whose own CI is red as a size-1 conflict.
  * **max_evaluations** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)]) – Budgets; partial results are
    always returned.
  * **max_seconds** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)]) – Budgets; partial results are
    always returned.
  * **max_sets** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)]) – Budgets; partial results are
    always returned.
  * **reuse_worktree** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]) – Reuse one worktree for every evaluation instead of a
    fresh one, so an expensive setup step (`npm install`, a build
    cache) is paid once rather than per evaluation. Pair it with
    [`mergeset.validation.staged_validation()`](_autosummary/mergeset.validation.html.md#mergeset.validation.staged_validation).
  * **on_event** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Callable)[[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str), [`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)], [`None`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)]]) – `(event, payload)` progress callback.
* **Return type:**
  [`Analysis`](_autosummary/mergeset.analysis.html.md#mergeset.analysis.Analysis)
* **Returns:**
  An [`Analysis`](_autosummary/mergeset.analysis.html.md#mergeset.analysis.Analysis).

### mergeset.analysis.unmatched_log_notes(log, , label='')

Say how many rows a pinned log is keeping but not using, and why.

Rows about other commits are never dropped, and never silently ignored
either: a re-run that is suddenly slow should say it is because heads moved.

* **Return type:**
  [`List`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.List)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]


# _autosummary/mergeset.attribution.html.md

# mergeset.attribution

From a failure to the changes that probably caused it.

When a set fails, the expensive information has already been paid for: the
runner said *what* failed. Turning that into “which of these changes did it”
saves the conflict-shrinking step several oracle calls, and on real failures it
lands directly on the culprit.

Three signals, in increasing order of how much they prove:

1. **Paths in the failure block.** Every path a failure mentions, not only the
   failing test’s own file — a stack trace’s actionable frame is usually a
   *source* file, and when a suite fails to load there are no test ids at all.
2. **The changes that touched those paths.** File-level attribution, the obvious
   move, and by itself frequently wrong: a drift test added by one change fails
   because of what a *different* change did to the sources it derives from.
3. **Identifiers named in the failure.** When the output quotes symbols — an
   assertion diff, an undefined name, a missing export — matching those against
   each candidate’s diff finds the change that introduced them even when it
   shares no file with the failing test. This is the only signal that gets that
   drift case right.

Everything here is a *hint*. A wrong hint costs the search one wasted check and
then it falls back to unguided shrinking; it never decides a verdict.

### Functions

| [`failure_text`](_autosummary/mergeset.attribution.html.md#mergeset.attribution.failure_text)(outcome)                          | Everything a validation outcome said, as one blob to mine.                                                         |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`git_diff_reader`](_autosummary/mergeset.attribution.html.md#mergeset.attribution.git_diff_reader)(repo, base, heads)             | A `diff_of` for [`suspects()`](_autosummary/mergeset.attribution.html.md#mergeset.attribution.suspects), reading (and caching) real git diffs. |
| [`identifiers_in`](_autosummary/mergeset.attribution.html.md#mergeset.attribution.identifiers_in)(text)                           | Camel/Pascal-case identifiers named in the failure output.                                                         |
| [`paths_in`](_autosummary/mergeset.attribution.html.md#mergeset.attribution.paths_in)(text)                                 | Every source-looking path mentioned, vendor directories excluded.                                                  |
| [`suspects`](_autosummary/mergeset.attribution.html.md#mergeset.attribution.suspects)(outcome, \*, files_by_change, within) | Changes the failure points at, or an empty set when it points nowhere.                                             |

### mergeset.attribution.failure_text(outcome)

Everything a validation outcome said, as one blob to mine.

* **Return type:**
  [`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)

### mergeset.attribution.git_diff_reader(repo, base, heads)

A `diff_of` for [`suspects()`](_autosummary/mergeset.attribution.html.md#mergeset.attribution.suspects), reading (and caching) real git diffs.

### mergeset.attribution.identifiers_in(text)

Camel/Pascal-case identifiers named in the failure output.

* **Return type:**
  [`List`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.List)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]

```pycon
>>> identifiers_in('+ "pointColorSeeds": { "$ref": "AxisDirectionType" }')
['pointColorSeeds', 'AxisDirectionType']
```

### mergeset.attribution.paths_in(text)

Every source-looking path mentioned, vendor directories excluded.

* **Return type:**
  [`List`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.List)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]

```pycon
>>> paths_in('FAIL tests/unit/a.test.ts [ tests/unit/a.test.ts ]')
['tests/unit/a.test.ts']
>>> paths_in(' at Module.x node_modules/zod/util.js:15 then src/schemas.ts:89:4')
['src/schemas.ts']
```

### mergeset.attribution.suspects(outcome, , files_by_change, within, diff_of=None)

Changes the failure points at, or an empty set when it points nowhere.

* **Parameters:**
  * **outcome** ([`ValidationOutcome`](_autosummary/mergeset.base.html.md#mergeset.base.ValidationOutcome)) – The failed validation, with whatever the runner printed.
  * **files_by_change** ([`Mapping`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Mapping)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str), [`Sequence`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Sequence)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]]) – Which files each change touched.
  * **within** ([`Iterable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Iterable)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]) – Only these changes are candidates (the set being evaluated).
  * **diff_of** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Callable)[[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)], [`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]]) – `change id -> its diff text`. Optional but valuable: it is
    what enables identifier matching, the only signal that attributes a
    failure to a change sharing no file with the failing test.
* **Return type:**
  [`frozenset`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#frozenset)
* **Returns:**
  A strict, non-empty subset of `within`, or `frozenset()` when the
  evidence is absent, useless, or implicates everything (in which case it
  has told us nothing and blind shrinking is the honest fallback).

```pycon
>>> out = ValidationOutcome(ok=False, failing_tests=['tests/a.test.ts::x'])
>>> set(suspects(out, files_by_change={'p1': ['tests/a.test.ts'], 'p2': ['b.ts']},
...              within=['p1', 'p2']))
{'p1'}
```


# _autosummary/mergeset.base.html.md

# mergeset.base

Core data structures and vocabulary of `mergeset`.

The unit of work is a **change**: a commit range `base..head`. Branches, pull
requests and explicit commit lists are merely *sources* that produce changes
(see [`mergeset.sources`](_autosummary/mergeset.sources.html.md#module-mergeset.sources)). Everything downstream — the evaluation log, the
solver, the report — speaks only of changes, identified by their string `id`.

A **change set** is a `frozenset` of change ids. Sets are the atoms the solver
reasons about; they are serialized as sorted lists so the JSONL log is stable
and diffable.

### Module Attributes

| [`UNKNOWN_FINGERPRINT`](_autosummary/mergeset.base.html.md#mergeset.base.UNKNOWN_FINGERPRINT)   | that is what rows written before fingerprints existed read back as, and the migration switch (`trust_unpinned`) must not adopt today's rows from an unknown validator as if they were old rows from a known one (#32).   |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`NO_RESOLVER`](_autosummary/mergeset.base.html.md#mergeset.base.NO_RESOLVER)           | What a row records as its resolver when conflicts were left unresolved (i2mint/mergeset#34).                                                                                                                             |
| [`MergeFn`](_autosummary/mergeset.base.html.md#mergeset.base.MergeFn)               | (changes to merge, in order) -> outcome + a tree to validate.                                                                                                                                                            |
| [`ValidateFn`](_autosummary/mergeset.base.html.md#mergeset.base.ValidateFn)            | (path to a merged worktree) -> outcome.                                                                                                                                                                                  |

### Functions

|--------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|

### *class* mergeset.base.Change(id, head, base, source='branch', weight=None, meta=<factory>)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

One candidate change: everything between `base` and `head`.

* **Parameters:**
  * **id** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – Short stable identifier, used everywhere else (log, report, CLI).
  * **head** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – Commit-ish holding the change (branch name, sha, PR head).
  * **base** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – Commit-ish the change is measured against.
  * **source** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – Which source produced it (`'branch'`, `'pr'`, `'commit'`).
  * **weight** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)]) – Cost of *dropping* this change. The solver drops the cheapest
    changes it can when it must drop something, so a high weight means
    “keep me”. `None` means “let the weighting policy decide”.
  * **meta** ([`Mapping`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Mapping)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str), [`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)]) – Source-specific extras (PR number, author, CI status, draft flag…).

```pycon
>>> c = Change(id='fix-a', head='origin/fix-a', base='origin/main')
>>> c.id, c.source
('fix-a', 'branch')
```

### *class* mergeset.base.Evaluation(subset, verdict, stage=None, merge=None, validation=None, duration=0.0, at=None, note='', base_sha=None, heads=<factory>, validator=None, resolver=None, cached=False)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

One row of the evaluation log — the single source of truth.

Everything else (conflict set, known-good/known-bad closure, merge plan,
reports) is *derived* from a sequence of these and is re-derivable.

A row is about the commits that were actually merged, not about the ids:
`base_sha` and `heads` (change id -> head sha) pin it to them, so a row
written before a branch was rewritten is never mistaken for an answer about
the rewritten branch (i2mint/mergeset#23). Rows written before pinning
existed carry neither and read back as *unpinned*; see
[`mergeset.log.EvaluationLog`](_autosummary/mergeset.log.html.md#mergeset.log.EvaluationLog). `validator` pins it to what was run
on that tree, the same way (i2mint/mergeset#32): the same commits under a
different test command are a different question.

#### base_sha *: [str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str) | [None](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)* *= None*

Full sha of the base the set was merged onto. `None` on unpinned rows.

#### cached *: [bool](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)* *= False*

True when this came from the log rather than from a real run. Not
serialized: it is a fact about *this* lookup, not about the evaluation.

#### *classmethod* from_jdict(d)

Inverse of [`to_jdict()`](_autosummary/mergeset.base.html.md#mergeset.base.Evaluation.to_jdict).

* **Return type:**
  [`Evaluation`](_autosummary/mergeset.base.html.md#mergeset.base.Evaluation)

#### heads *: [Mapping](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Mapping)[[str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str), [str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]*

Full head sha of each change in `subset` when it was evaluated.

#### *property* merge_dependent *: [bool](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)*

True iff how conflicts were resolved decided this row’s outcome.

An assisted merge exists only because a resolver resolved it; a
textual conflict stands only because none did. A clean merge is the
same tree whatever the resolver, so its verdict answers any of them.

```pycon
>>> Evaluation(frozenset('a'), Verdict.PASS).merge_dependent
False
>>> Evaluation(frozenset('a'), Verdict.PASS,
...            merge=MergeOutcome(True, assisted=True)).merge_dependent
True
>>> Evaluation(frozenset('ab'), Verdict.FAIL,
...            merge=MergeOutcome(False, 'conflict')).merge_dependent
True
```

#### *property* ok *: [bool](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)*

True iff the set evaluated as good.

#### *property* pinned *: [bool](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)*

True iff the row records which commits it was evaluated against.

#### resolver *: [str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str) | [None](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)* *= None*

Fingerprint of how conflicts were resolved when the set was merged
([`NO_RESOLVER`](_autosummary/mergeset.base.html.md#mergeset.base.NO_RESOLVER), or [`mergeset.oracle.resolver_fingerprint_of()`](_autosummary/mergeset.oracle.html.md#mergeset.oracle.resolver_fingerprint_of)).
`None` on rows written before i2mint/mergeset#34. It matters only on a
row whose outcome the resolver decided: see [`merge_dependent`](_autosummary/mergeset.base.html.md#mergeset.base.Evaluation.merge_dependent).

#### to_jdict()

JSON-able view; `subset` becomes a sorted list.

* **Return type:**
  [`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)

#### *property* unresolved_conflict *: [bool](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)*

True iff the row is a textual conflict that no resolver resolved.

#### validator *: [str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str) | [None](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)* *= None*

Fingerprint of the validator that judged the tree (see
[`mergeset.validation.fingerprint_of()`](_autosummary/mergeset.validation.html.md#mergeset.validation.fingerprint_of)). `None` on rows written
before fingerprints, and on rows judged by a validator that has none.

This is *the* expensive seam: one call is typically a merge plus a test run.

### *class* mergeset.base.MergeOutcome(ok, reason='conflict', conflicting_files=(), assisted=False, assist_diff=None, order=(), detail='', resolved_commit=None)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Result of merging a change set onto its base.

`reason` is load-bearing. “These changes conflict with each other” and “we
could not run the experiment” are completely different facts, and conflating
them is how a run reports *0 of 15 mergeable, complete* with total
confidence when the real problem was a bad worktree path. Only
`reason == 'conflict'` may ever enter the conflict set; an `'error'`
aborts, because a set that was never tested has told us nothing.

#### reason *: [str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)* *= 'conflict'*

`'conflict'` (a real textual conflict) or `'error'` (the merge could
not be attempted: bad path, missing ref, unusable worktree).

#### resolved_commit *: [str](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str) | [None](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)* *= None*

base plus every head,
conflicts resolved. A deeper tier checks this commit out instead of
asking the resolver again (i2mint/mergeset#30). Not in [`to_jdict()`](_autosummary/mergeset.base.html.md#mergeset.base.MergeOutcome.to_jdict):
[`Evaluation.to_jdict()`](_autosummary/mergeset.base.html.md#mergeset.base.Evaluation.to_jdict) stores it beside `merge`, because releases
before #30 build `MergeOutcome(**merge)` and would refuse the log.

* **Type:**
  The merge commit an assisted resolution produced

#### to_jdict()

JSON-able view (without [`resolved_commit`](_autosummary/mergeset.base.html.md#mergeset.base.MergeOutcome.resolved_commit); see there).

* **Return type:**
  [`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)

```pycon
...                                 StageRun('test', 6.0, 0)]).stage_seconds
{'test': 6.0}
```

# _autosummary/mergeset.cli.html.md

# mergeset.cli

Command line surface.

The durable part is `_dispatch_funcs` — a plain list of plain functions. Only
the last line binds it to an adapter, so the library stays free of any CLI
library and a second surface (HTTP, MCP) is the same list projected differently.

Note the deliberate absence of `from __future__ import annotations`: it turns
every hint into a string, and the CLI adapter reads the real annotations to
decide that `--max-seconds` is a float rather than the string `"600"`.

### mergeset.cli.branches(branch, , repo='.', base='HEAD', validate_command=None, validate_stage=None, validate_fingerprint=None, validate_optional=None, validate_input=None, merge_only=False, tier=None, tier_cost=None, timeout=None, retries=0, max_evaluations=None, max_seconds=None, max_sets=None, confirm_budget_seconds=None, confirm_max_runs=None, confirm_max_sets=None, must_include=None, log_path=None, trust_unpinned_log=False, report_dir=None, report_format=None, integration_branches=False, reuse_worktree=None, resolver='none', no_pairwise=False, no_decompose=False, quiet=False)

Find maximal mergeable sets among the given branches.

* **Parameters:**
  * **branch** ([`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]) – Branch names, as positional arguments.
  * **repo** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – Path to the git repository.
  * **base** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – What to merge onto.
  * **validate_command** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]) – Shell command that validates a merged tree.
    Default: a fail-fast pytest run.
  * **validate_stage** ([`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)) – `'name:command'`, repeatable, in order — the way to
    describe a project whose validation is a sequence rather than one
    command (install, then build, then test, then lint). Each stage
    reports its own exit code, so “failed to build” stays
    distinguishable from “tests failed”. Overrides –validate-command.
  * **validate_fingerprint** ([`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)) – `'stage:path'`, repeatable — skip that stage
    unless the file’s contents changed. Point it at a lockfile and a
    slow dependency install is paid once per run instead of once per
    evaluation (pair it with –reuse-worktree).
  * **validate_optional** ([`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)) – Stage name, repeatable — its failure is recorded but
    does not veto the set. Use it for a lint pass the project treats as
    advisory.
  * **validate_input** ([`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)) – Path, repeatable — a file (or directory) outside the
    repository that the validation runs, such as the script in
    `--validate-command 'python ~/checks/smoke.py'`. Its contents join
    the validator’s fingerprint, so editing it retires the verdicts the
    old version gave; without it, only the command’s text counts. Files
    inside the repository need no flag: the commits pin them. Applies
    to every tier.
  * **merge_only** ([`bool`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)) – Skip validation entirely; only textual mergeability counts.
  * **tier** ([`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)) – `'name:command'`, repeatable, ordered cheapest-first — tiered
    validation: the first tier screens every candidate set, and each
    later tier only confirms the sets its predecessor left standing, so
    an expensive suite runs on a handful of sets instead of dozens. A
    tier is ONE validator with its OWN evaluation log (a cheap PASS is
    not evidence about an expensive tier). `--validate-stage`
    composes stages *inside* one validator; `--tier` composes
    validators. To make the staged validator a tier, give its name
    bare: `--validate-stage 'build:make' 'test:make test' --tier
    unit 'e2e:make e2e'`. Tier logs live in the artifact store next
    to the default log, one per tier, so –log-path is refused here.
    –tier takes every value after it: put branch names first.
  * **tier_cost** ([`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)) – `'tier:seconds'`, repeatable — the declared cost of one
    run, used until the tier has been timed. Set it for a tier that has
    never run, or it is scheduled as if it were cheap.
  * **timeout** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)]) – Seconds allowed per validation run (per tier, with –tier).
  * **retries** ([`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – Re-run a failing validation this many times before believing it.
  * **max_evaluations** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)]) – Stop after this many expensive evaluations (with
    –tier, these three bound the screening tier).
  * **max_seconds** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)]) – Stop after this much wall time.
  * **max_sets** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)]) – Stop after finding this many maximal sets.
  * **confirm_budget_seconds** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)]) – With –tier: seconds each deeper tier may
    spend. Runs are admitted on the pessimistic estimate, so the budget
    is not overrun on a guess.
  * **confirm_max_runs** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)]) – With –tier: at most this many runs per deeper tier;
    wins over the budget when both are given.
  * **confirm_max_sets** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)]) – With –tier: stop a deeper tier after confirming this
    many maximal sets (`1`: just the best plan, cheaply).
  * **must_include** ([`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)) – Change id, repeatable (a branch name, or `pr12` for

  * **log_path** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]) – Evaluation log (JSONL). Default:

    (`<artifact root>/reports/<repo-slug>/`), never into the
    analysed repository — see [`mergeset.storage`](_autosummary/mergeset.storage.html.md#module-mergeset.storage).
  * **integration_branches** ([`bool`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)) – Create a local `integration/*` branch per maximal set.
  * **reuse_worktree** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]) – Absolute path to one git worktree to check every

Print what the evaluation log already knows, without evaluating anything.

Use this to answer questions about a finished run: the log is the single
source of truth, so re-deriving what it already says costs a reader’s trust.

well as the log, so it is a library call — `markdown_report(analysis)` —
not a command that could pretend the log alone is enough.)

# _autosummary/mergeset.cost.html.md

# mergeset.cost

What an evaluation costs — per validation tier, and per change.

Until now `mergeset` treated every evaluation as costing the same: one suite
run. That is true only while there is one suite. As soon as validation is
*tiered* — a fast unit run, then a slow end-to-end run needing containers, a
database and a browser — the search is choosing between evaluations that differ
by two orders of magnitude, and it cannot choose well while it is told they are
the same.

So cost becomes an **input**, on the same footing as the changes and the base.
It is one keyword argument, and its default is measured rather than declared:
the evaluation log already records the wall-clock duration of everything that
has ever been run, so [`cost_from_log()`](_autosummary/mergeset.cost.html.md#mergeset.cost.cost_from_log) reads back data the package has been
storing all along.

\*\*A cost model over CI timings has at least two regimes, because caching is what
makes CI affordable.\*\* On a real run the base check — the empty set, evaluated
before anything else — took 51.2 s, while the nine candidate sets took 27.2 to
37.2 s. The base check is not a small candidate set: it is the first evaluation,
so it is the one that always pays the cold dependency install that every later
evaluation skips through a fingerprinted setup stage. It sits at the extreme of
the independent variable (size 0) *and* is the slowest run, which is exactly the
shape that dominates a linear fit: fit one line through both regimes and the
slope comes out **negative**, i.e. the model concludes that adding changes makes
validation faster. Budgets survive that, because the residual is enormous.
Ordering does not — and a wrong budget is visible where a wrong order is not.

Hence [`MeasuredCost.central()`](_autosummary/mergeset.cost.html.md#mergeset.cost.MeasuredCost.central): the slope is fitted on the body only, the
empty set is priced from its own regime instead of being extrapolated, and a
negative fitted slope degrades to the mean because adding a change cannot make
validation faster.

Two estimates, not one, because they answer different questions:

- [`estimate()`](_autosummary/mergeset.cost.html.md#mergeset.cost.MeasuredCost.estimate) — the central estimate, used for **ordering**.
- [`pessimistic()`](_autosummary/mergeset.cost.html.md#mergeset.cost.MeasuredCost.pessimistic) — plus the worst residual against that same
  model, used for **budget admission**, because overrunning a budget is a worse
  failure than deferring one evaluation. What it carries is the spread *within*
  a regime — an install that ran because the lockfile moved, a slow runner — and
  never a stand-in for a regime that should have been separated. The expensive
  regime is priced where it occurs and reserved explicitly instead; see
  `mergeset.tiers._runs_allowed`.

Held as a hypothesis rather than a law: on the only data available the body was
remarkably **flat** — sd 3.1 s across set sizes 1 to 13, against a 27 s floor —
so set size may barely predict cost at all, and the slope may be modelling
noise. Nine points on one repository is not enough to drop it (a validator that
selects tests per change would genuinely have a slope), but it is enough to say
that the reserve is load-bearing and the fit is not yet demonstrated to be.

### Module Attributes

| [`UNMEASURED_TIER_SECONDS`](_autosummary/mergeset.cost.html.md#mergeset.cost.UNMEASURED_TIER_SECONDS)   | What one evaluation of a tier is assumed to cost when nothing is known about it — nothing measured, nothing declared.   |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`Seconds`](_autosummary/mergeset.cost.html.md#mergeset.cost.Seconds)                   | total seconds, or a per-stage breakdown that is summed.                                                                 |

### Functions

| [`cost_from_log`](_autosummary/mergeset.cost.html.md#mergeset.cost.cost_from_log)(log, \*, tier[, declared, ...])   | Seed a cost model from an existing evaluation log — the real default.   |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`set_cost`](_autosummary/mergeset.cost.html.md#mergeset.cost.set_cost)(cost_model, tiers, subset, \*[, ...])  | What it costs to take `subset` all the way down `tiers`.                |

### Classes

### *class* mergeset.cost.CostModel(\*args, \*\*kwargs)

Bases: [`Protocol`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Protocol)

What the scheduler needs to know about price.

Any object with these four methods is a cost model: a table of declared
constants, a model fitted to the log, or something that queries a CI
provider’s historical timings.

#### estimate(tier, subset)

Central estimate, in seconds. Used to *order* candidate work.

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

#### is_measured(tier)

Whether this tier’s estimate rests on observation or on a guess.

* **Return type:**
  [`bool`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)

#### observe(tier, subset, seconds)

Record what an evaluation cost, so the next estimate is better.

`seconds` is a total, or a per-stage mapping that is summed.

* **Return type:**
  [`None`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)

#### pessimistic(tier, subset)

Upper estimate, in seconds. Used to *admit* work against a budget.

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

### *class* mergeset.cost.MeasuredCost(declared=<factory>, per_change=<factory>, unmeasured_seconds=60.0)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

A per-tier cost model fitted to observations, backed by declarations.

* **Parameters:**
  * **declared** ([`Mapping`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Mapping)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str), [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)]) – `tier -> seconds`, used until that tier has been observed.
    This is how a tier nobody has ever run gets a sane price: the person
    adding it usually knows roughly what it costs.
  * **per_change** ([`Mapping`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Mapping)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str), [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)]) – `change id -> extra seconds` this change adds to any
    evaluation containing it. The per-change half of the model, for the
    case where one candidate is known to be much heavier than the rest.
    Default: nothing, and the fitted slope carries the average
    per-change cost instead.
  * **unmeasured_seconds** ([`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)) – Price of a tier with neither observations nor a
    declaration. See [`UNMEASURED_TIER_SECONDS`](_autosummary/mergeset.cost.html.md#mergeset.cost.UNMEASURED_TIER_SECONDS).

```pycon
>>> cost = MeasuredCost(declared={'e2e': 300.0})
>>> cost.estimate('e2e', frozenset({'a'}))
300.0
>>> cost.is_measured('e2e')
False
>>> cost.observe('unit', frozenset({'a'}), 10.0)
>>> cost.observe('unit', frozenset({'a', 'b', 'c'}), 20.0)
>>> cost.observe('unit', frozenset({'a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e'}), 30.0)
>>> cost.estimate('unit', frozenset({'a', 'b', 'c', 'd'}))
25.0
>>> cost.is_measured('unit')
True
```

An unknown tier is priced, not free — otherwise a cost-ordered scheduler
would run it first, precisely because nobody has ever timed it:

```pycon
>>> cost.estimate('nobody-timed-this', frozenset({'a'}))
60.0
```

The base check is read from its own regime rather than extrapolated:

```pycon
>>> cold = MeasuredCost()
>>> cold.observe('unit', frozenset(), 51.2)                  # base, cold
>>> for n in range(1, 10):
...     cold.observe('unit', frozenset(range(n)), 30.0 + n / 10)
>>> round(cold.estimate('unit', frozenset()), 1)             # its own regime
51.2
>>> round(cold.estimate('unit', frozenset(range(9))), 1)     # the body's
30.9
```

#### central(tier, size)

Seconds for a set of `size` at `tier`, before per-change extras.

The one place the model lives, so [`estimate()`](_autosummary/mergeset.cost.html.md#mergeset.cost.MeasuredCost.estimate) and
[`pessimistic()`](_autosummary/mergeset.cost.html.md#mergeset.cost.MeasuredCost.pessimistic) cannot drift apart.

Never below the fastest run ever observed for the tier. An evaluation
that has never taken less than 27 s will not take 0 s, and a floor of
zero is not merely inaccurate: it makes a budget check divide by nothing
and conclude the tier is unlimited.

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

#### estimate(tier, subset)

Central estimate of what evaluating `subset` at `tier` will cost.

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

```pycon
>>> cost = MeasuredCost(declared={'unit': 10.0}, per_change={'x': -50.0})
>>> cost.estimate('unit', frozenset({'x'}))
0.0
```

#### forget(tier)

Drop this tier’s observations, so a caller can re-ingest a log.

* **Return type:**
  [`None`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)

#### is_measured(tier)

True iff this tier’s estimate comes from observations.

* **Return type:**
  [`bool`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)

#### observe(tier, subset, seconds)

Record one real timing, as a total or a per-stage breakdown.

* **Return type:**
  [`None`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)

#### pessimistic(tier, subset)

Upper estimate: the central one plus the worst residual ever seen.

With no observations there is no residual to add and this is the central
estimate — the honest position, not an optimistic one: the declared or
unmeasured number is already the only thing known.

Note what this is *not* doing. The cold base check is priced by its own
regime (see [`central()`](_autosummary/mergeset.cost.html.md#mergeset.cost.MeasuredCost.central)), so it contributes no residual here. What
this carries is the spread *within* a regime, which is the variance no
candidate set predicts. The expensive regime is reserved explicitly by
the scheduler instead of being smuggled in as a hedge.

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

```pycon
>>> cost = MeasuredCost()
>>> cost.observe('unit', frozenset({'a'}), 45.0)
>>> cost.observe('unit', frozenset({'a'}), 80.0)   # the lockfile moved
>>> round(cost.estimate('unit', frozenset({'a'})), 1)
62.5
>>> round(cost.pessimistic('unit', frozenset({'a'})), 1)
80.0
```

#### runs(tier)

How many timings this tier’s estimate rests on.

* **Return type:**
  [`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)

#### summary()

Per-tier view of the model, for a report to print.

Says what the number is *and where it came from*, because an estimate
with no provenance is indistinguishable from a magic constant. This is
the published view of the evidence; the observation list itself is
private, so its shape can change without breaking callers.

* **Return type:**
  [`Dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Dict)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str), [`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)]

### mergeset.cost.Seconds

total seconds, or a per-stage breakdown that is
summed. The mapping form exists so that recording per-stage durations
(i2mint/mergeset#17) lands as *data* rather than as a change to a published
signature — the regime this module infers today is one a breakdown states.

* **Type:**
  What one evaluation cost

alias of [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float) | [`Mapping`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Mapping)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str), [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)]

### mergeset.cost.UNMEASURED_TIER_SECONDS *= 60.0*

What one evaluation of a tier is assumed to cost when nothing is known about
it — nothing measured, nothing declared. It is the first run of a brand new
tier, and the honest answer is “we do not know yet”.

One minute is chosen to be *wrong in the safe direction*: large enough that a
cost-ordered scheduler puts an unknown tier after every tier it has actually
timed, small enough that a first run still gets scheduled at all. `inf`
would be safer still and would mean no new tier ever runs a first time, which
is not a cost model but a refusal. Override it with one keyword argument.

### mergeset.cost.cost_from_log(log, , tier, declared=None, per_change=None, unmeasured_seconds=60.0)

Seed a cost model from an existing evaluation log — the real default.

Every row of the log already carries `subset` and `duration`, so the
price of the tier that produced that log is not a thing anyone needs to
declare: it has been measured, repeatedly, and thrown away. This reads it
back.

`tier` names which tier those rows belong to, because the log itself does
not say — one log holds one tier’s rows by construction
(see [`mergeset.tiers`](_autosummary/mergeset.tiers.html.md#module-mergeset.tiers)).

* **Return type:**
  [`MeasuredCost`](_autosummary/mergeset.cost.html.md#mergeset.cost.MeasuredCost)

```pycon
>>> from mergeset.base import Evaluation, Verdict
>>> rows = [Evaluation(frozenset({'a'}), Verdict.PASS, duration=40.0),
...         Evaluation(frozenset({'a', 'b', 'c'}), Verdict.FAIL, duration=60.0)]
>>> cost = cost_from_log(rows, tier='unit')
>>> cost.estimate('unit', frozenset({'a', 'b'}))
50.0
```

### mergeset.cost.set_cost(cost_model, tiers, subset, , pessimistic=False)

What it costs to take `subset` all the way down `tiers`.

The tiers run in order and every one of them runs, so the price of a full
verdict is their sum — which is exactly what makes a cheap first tier worth
having: most sets never reach the second term.

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

```pycon
>>> cost = MeasuredCost(declared={'unit': 45.0, 'e2e': 300.0})
>>> set_cost(cost, ['unit', 'e2e'], frozenset({'a'}))
345.0
```


# _autosummary/mergeset.gitops.html.md

# mergeset.gitops

Git primitives: the cheap pre-oracles and the isolated merge.

Two very different costs live here, and keeping them apart is the point:

- **Cheap** (milliseconds, no working tree): `git merge-tree --write-tree`
  answers “do these two changes conflict textually?” and `git diff --name-only`
  answers “which files does this change touch?”. Everything these two can decide
  must never reach the expensive oracle.
- **Expensive** (seconds to minutes): actually materializing a merged tree in a
  throwaway worktree so a test suite can run on it.

### Module Attributes

| [`MIN_GIT_VERSION`](_autosummary/mergeset.gitops.html.md#mergeset.gitops.MIN_GIT_VERSION)   | `git merge-tree --write-tree` needs this; it is also when `--merge-base` landed.   |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

### Functions

| [`changed_files`](_autosummary/mergeset.gitops.html.md#mergeset.gitops.changed_files)(repo, base, head)                  | Files a change touches, as `git diff --name-only base...head`.           |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`check_git_capability`](_autosummary/mergeset.gitops.html.md#mergeset.gitops.check_git_capability)()                           | Raise a fixable error if git is missing or too old for `merge-tree`.     |
| [`create_integration_branch`](_autosummary/mergeset.gitops.html.md#mergeset.gitops.create_integration_branch)(repo, name, base, ...) | Create a local branch holding `base` + all heads, for manual testing.    |
| [`git`](_autosummary/mergeset.gitops.html.md#mergeset.gitops.git)(repo, \*args[, check, timeout])              | Run `git -C repo *args` and capture its output.                          |
| [`git_version`](_autosummary/mergeset.gitops.html.md#mergeset.gitops.git_version)()                                    | The installed git version as a tuple, e.g. `(2, 50, 1)`.                 |
| [`is_ancestor`](_autosummary/mergeset.gitops.html.md#mergeset.gitops.is_ancestor)(repo, ancestor, descendant)          | True iff `ancestor` is reachable from `descendant` (or equal to it).     |
| [`merge_base`](_autosummary/mergeset.gitops.html.md#mergeset.gitops.merge_base)(repo, a, b)                           | Best common ancestor of `a` and `b`.                                     |

| [`pairwise_textual_conflicts`](_autosummary/mergeset.gitops.html.md#mergeset.gitops.pairwise_textual_conflicts)(repo, base, heads)    | Yield `(id_a, id_b, files)` for every pair that conflicts textually.     |

| [`textual_conflict`](_autosummary/mergeset.gitops.html.md#mergeset.gitops.textual_conflict)(repo, base, head_a, head_b)     | Conflicting files if merging both heads onto `base` clashes textually.   |

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

### mergeset.gitops.changed_files(repo, base, head)

Files a change touches, as `git diff --name-only base...head`.

The three-dot form is deliberate: it compares against the merge base, so a
change is measured by what *it* did, not by what happened on base meanwhile.

* **Return type:**
  [`List`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.List)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]

### mergeset.gitops.check_git_capability()

Raise a fixable error if git is missing or too old for `merge-tree`.

* **Return type:**
  [`None`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)

### mergeset.gitops.create_integration_branch(repo, name, base, heads, , force=False)

Create a local branch holding `base` + all heads, for manual testing.

Only ever creates *new* local branches. Never touches an existing branch
unless `force` is passed explicitly, and never pushes anything.

* **Return type:**
  [`Tuple`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Tuple)[[`bool`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool), [`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]
* **Returns:**
  `(created, message)`.

Run `git -C repo *args` and capture its output.

* **Return type:**

```pycon
>>> git('.', 'rev-parse', '--git-dir').ok in (True, False)
True
```

### mergeset.gitops.git_version()

The installed git version as a tuple, e.g. `(2, 50, 1)`.

* **Return type:**
  [`Tuple`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Tuple)[[`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int), [`...`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#Ellipsis)]

### mergeset.gitops.is_ancestor(repo, ancestor, descendant)

True iff `ancestor` is reachable from `descendant` (or equal to it).

* **Return type:**
  [`bool`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)

### mergeset.gitops.merge_base(repo, a, b)

Best common ancestor of `a` and `b`.

* **Return type:**
  [`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)

### mergeset.gitops.merge_sequence(repo, base, heads)

Merge every head onto `base`, one at a time, without any worktree.

The mechanic, which is the cheap heart of the whole tool:

```default
acc = base
for each head:
    tree = git merge-tree --write-tree acc head   # conflict -> non-zero
    acc  = git commit-tree tree -p acc -p head
```

`n` `merge-tree` calls of a few milliseconds each, no checkout, no
working tree, and — when it comes out clean — a real commit that a worktree
can be checked out from only if we actually intend to run tests on it.

Every merge is measured against the accumulated result rather than pairwise,
which is what keeps a stale branch from manufacturing false conflicts.

* **Return type:**
  [`SequenceMerge`](_autosummary/mergeset.gitops.html.md#mergeset.gitops.SequenceMerge)

### mergeset.gitops.merged_worktree(repo, base, heads, , root=None, keep=False, reuse=None)

Materialize `base` plus every head in a worktree, ready for validation.

The merge itself happens in the object database ([`merge_sequence()`](_autosummary/mergeset.gitops.html.md#mergeset.gitops.merge_sequence)), so
a conflicted set costs milliseconds and never touches the filesystem at all.
Only a *clean* set gets checked out — which is the only case where anything
wanted to run tests anyway.

Yields `(worktree_path, outcome)`. On a conflict the path is `None` and
the outcome names the change that failed (`outcome.order[-1]`) and the
conflicting files — that attribution is what lets the solver shrink straight
to the suspects instead of halving blindly.

* **Parameters:**
  **reuse** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]) – An existing worktree to check the merge commit out into, instead
  of creating a fresh one. This is the seam that makes expensive
  per-tree setup (`npm install`, a virtualenv, a build cache)
  survive across evaluations; see
  [`mergeset.validation.staged_validation()`](_autosummary/mergeset.validation.html.md#mergeset.validation.staged_validation).
* **Return type:**
  [`Iterator`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Iterator)[[`Tuple`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Tuple)[[`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)], [`MergeOutcome`](_autosummary/mergeset.base.html.md#mergeset.base.MergeOutcome)]]

### mergeset.gitops.pairwise_textual_conflicts(repo, base, heads)

Yield `(id_a, id_b, files)` for every pair that conflicts textually.

`heads` maps change id -> commit-ish. This is the pre-oracle that buys the
most: every pair it finds is a size-2 conflict known before any test runs.
Each pair is merged *onto base*, never against each other — see
[`textual_conflict()`](_autosummary/mergeset.gitops.html.md#mergeset.gitops.textual_conflict) for why that distinction is not cosmetic.

* **Return type:**
  [`Iterator`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Iterator)[[`Tuple`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Tuple)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str), [`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str), [`List`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.List)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]]]

### mergeset.gitops.persistent_worktree(repo, base, path)

Create (once) a worktree meant to be reused across many evaluations.

Reusing one tree is what makes an expensive setup step amortizable: install
dependencies once, then check out each candidate merge into the same
directory. Returns `path`.

* **Return type:**
  [`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)

### mergeset.gitops.resolve(repo, rev)

Full sha of `rev`.

* **Raises:**
  [**CapabilityError**](_autosummary/mergeset.html.md#mergeset.CapabilityError) – if the revision cannot be resolved in `repo`.
* **Return type:**
  [`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)

### mergeset.gitops.singleton_textual_conflicts(repo, base, heads)

Yield `(id, files)` for every change that will not even merge onto base.

The cheapest check there is, and on real PR sets it fires more than you would
expect: a PR opened against a base branch that has since moved on is green on
GitHub and still unmergeable onto the base you actually care about.

* **Return type:**
  [`Iterator`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Iterator)[[`Tuple`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Tuple)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str), [`List`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.List)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]]]

### mergeset.gitops.textual_conflict(repo, base, head_a, head_b)

Conflicting files if merging both heads onto `base` clashes textually.

\*\*This chains through `base` on purpose.\*\* Plain `git merge-tree A B`
merges using `merge-base(A, B)`, which is *not* `base` whenever the two
branches were cut at different times — and then it reports base’s own
commits as conflicts. On a real 15-PR set that mistake produced 13
“conflicting” pairs where only 2 were real (measured by TEST on
a real trial). So we merge A onto base first, in the object database, and ask
whether B then conflicts with *that*.

* **Return type:**
  [`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`List`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.List)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]]
* **Returns:**
  `None` when the merge is clean, otherwise the list of conflicted paths
  (possibly empty if git reported a conflict it could not attribute).


# _autosummary/mergeset.html.md

# mergeset

Which of these branches can be merged together?

Given a base commit and *n* candidate changes (branches, PRs, commits),
`mergeset` finds the **maximal sets** that merge cleanly and still pass
validation — and the minimal **conflicts** that stop the rest.

The simple case is one call:

```default
from mergeset import analyze, branch_changes, markdown_report

changes = list(branch_changes('.', ['feature-a', 'feature-b'], base='main'))
analysis = analyze('.', changes)
print(markdown_report(analysis))
```

Everything expensive is cached in an append-only JSONL log, so a second run
costs nothing for sets already decided, and the cheap oracles (per-change CI
status, `git merge-tree` textual conflicts, file-overlap decomposition) run
first so that most answers never cost a test run at all.

Every piece is one keyword argument away from being replaced: where changes come
from (`mergeset.sources`), how a set is merged and validated
(`mergeset.oracle`, `mergeset.validation`), how the search spends its budget
(`mergeset.solve`), how results are rendered (`mergeset.report`), and where
artifacts are kept (`mergeset.storage`).

Everything mergeset produces — reports, evaluation logs, captured validation
output, fixtures — is derived from whatever repository was analysed, so it goes
to an artifact store rooted at `~/.local/share/mergeset/<kind>/` and **never**
into a repository. Point that store at S3 with one keyword argument; no caller
changes.

### Functions

| [`analyze`](_autosummary/mergeset.html.md#mergeset.analyze)(repo, changes, \*[, base, validate, ...])   | Find the maximal sets of `changes` that merge and validate on `base`.                                                      |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`skills_dir`](_autosummary/mergeset.html.md#mergeset.skills_dir)()                                        | The directory of skills bundled inside the installed package.                                                              |
| [`install_skills`](_autosummary/mergeset.html.md#mergeset.install_skills)([target, skills_root, link, ...])    | Put the bundled skills where an agent host will find them.                                                                 |
| [`bundled_skills`](_autosummary/mergeset.html.md#mergeset.bundled_skills)([skills_root])                       | Yield the directory of every bundled skill (each holding a `SKILL.md`).                                                    |
| [`analyze_tiered`](_autosummary/mergeset.html.md#mergeset.analyze_tiered)(repo, changes, \*, tiers[, ...])     | Screen with the cheap tier, confirm the frontier with the expensive ones.                                                  |
| [`anytime_answer`](_autosummary/mergeset.html.md#mergeset.anytime_answer)(change_ids, conflicts, \*, ...)      | The best validated set so far, plus a sound bound on what is being missed.                                                 |
| [`best_set_including`](_autosummary/mergeset.html.md#mergeset.best_set_including)(change_ids, evaluate, \*, ...)   | The heaviest validated set that **contains** every change in `must_include`.                                               |
| [`chained_evaluate`](_autosummary/mergeset.html.md#mergeset.chained_evaluate)(evaluators)                        | Compose per-tier evaluators into one, short-circuiting on the first failure.                                               |
